segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 1: Checking Writing Class Enrolment at the Community Centre

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Hi, Daniel. Thanks for meeting me at the community centre. I'm checking the writing course before I choose a group. I also need a short chart summary for our club newsletter. Does this chart count teachers?

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: No. It shows the number of students in three writing classes over four weeks. I help with class bookings, so I can explain it.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Which group is which?

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: Class A is the beginner group. Class B is intermediate, and Class C is advanced. The vertical axis shows student numbers from zero to thirty. These are enrolment counts, not the number who attended every lesson.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: What were the numbers in week one?

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: Class A had twenty students, Class B had fifteen, and Class C had ten. The total was forty-five.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Then B grew by three in week two, didn't it?

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: Yes. A stayed at twenty, B went up to eighteen, and C increased to twelve. In week three, Class A dropped to sixteen, Class B remained at eighteen, and Class C rose to fourteen.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: So A fell by four between weeks two and three. What happened in week four?

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: A went back up to nineteen, B fell to seventeen, and C stayed at fourteen.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Then B was the smallest at the end?

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: No, Class C was the smallest with fourteen. Class B had seventeen, while A was the largest with nineteen.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: How would you describe B's overall change?

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: Class B increased from fifteen to seventeen. That's a rise of two students overall. A ended one below its starting number, while C had the largest increase: four students.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: I also need C's share of the total in week four.

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: Nineteen plus seventeen plus fourteen makes fifty. Class C had fourteen out of fifty, so that's twenty-eight percent.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: And its share at the beginning?

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: Ten out of forty-five, or about twenty-two percent. So the proportion rose, even though A remained the largest class.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: I've written the title as 'Student Numbers by Class, Weeks 1–4'.

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: One correction: the title is 'Enrollment in Writing Classes, Weeks 1–4'. Please copy it exactly rather than replacing the first word.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Understood. Should I describe the numbers in the present tense?

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: Use the past tense for these class numbers because the data is from last month. You can still say 'the chart shows' when introducing the chart itself.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: And for trends, I can use increase, decrease, remain stable or fluctuate?

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: Yes, when the pattern fits. For comparisons, use 'compared with' or 'whereas'. For example, 'Class C increased, whereas Class A remained almost stable.' Avoid calling a changing figure exactly constant.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Thanks. I'll check every number before I send the newsletter paragraph.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 2: Planning a Community Art Project: Budget and Timeline

segments.speaker: Sarah
segments.text: Hello everyone. I'm Sarah, the community arts coordinator. This session is for residents interested in our spring art project. I'll explain the costs and dates before you decide whether to join. You do not need previous experience, and there is no charge for attending the workshops. Tickets are only needed for the exhibition opening.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: We have a total budget of £12,000. Of this, £5,000 is for materials, £4,000 for artist fees, and £3,000 for venue hire. Materials take the largest share, at about forty-two percent. Artist fees account for about thirty-three percent, and venue hire takes twenty-five percent. The first two percentages are rounded to the nearest whole number.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Last year, the total budget was £10,000. This year's total is £2,000 higher, which is a twenty percent increase. Materials have risen from £3,000 to £5,000, an increase of about sixty-seven percent. We are buying reusable equipment as well as paint and paper, so some items will remain available next year. Artist fees have gone from £3,500 to £4,000, a rise of about fourteen percent. Venue hire has fallen from £3,500 to £3,000, a drop of about fourteen percent. We negotiated the lower price by booking several dates together.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Our planning meeting will be on March 1. The first workshop will be on March 15. Workshops will then run every two weeks until the end of June. A session lasts two hours, with a short break halfway through. The final exhibition opens on July 10 and closes on July 24, after two weeks. Please arrive early for the first workshop so we can show you where to leave coats and bags.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: There will be eight workshops this year, compared with six last year. That is two additional sessions, or approximately thirty-three percent more. We expect two hundred people at the exhibition opening, up from one hundred and fifty last year. The hall holds two hundred and fifty people, so our expected opening attendance would fill eighty percent of its seats. This is a forecast, so we will check the actual number afterwards rather than report it as an achieved result.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: We have secured a grant of £2,000 from the local council. This covers two thirds of the £3,000 venue hire cost. The remaining £1,000 will come from ticket sales. We expect to sell two hundred opening tickets at £5 each, raising £1,000. Our other project funds come from savings and donations. Please contact the office if you want a written copy of the full budget.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Finally, registration opens tomorrow. Give your name and telephone number at the desk after this session. We will contact everyone a week before the first workshop to confirm the room and remind you to wear clothes suitable for painting. Thank you for coming.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 3: Reporting a Campus Bicycle Survey Accurately

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Today we'll use our simulated campus survey to practise reporting changes accurately. Leila and Marcus, your pilot study concerns bicycles parked outside two buildings, the library and the sports centre. You counted parked bicycles, not the number of students who cycled during an entire day. Keep that distinction in your report.

segments.speaker: Leila
segments.text: In the first survey, in March 2024, the weekday average outside the library was forty bicycles. The sports centre average was twenty. We repeated the counts in March 2025.

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: In the second survey, the library average was sixty and the sports centre average was thirty. I originally wrote that the library had grown twice as fast, because its increase was twenty bicycles and the sports centre's increase was only ten.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: That confuses absolute change with percentage change. The percentage increase was fifty percent at both sites. Twenty divided by forty is one half, just as ten divided by twenty is one half. A larger numerical increase does not necessarily mean a faster rate of growth.

segments.speaker: Leila
segments.text: Together, the second survey recorded an average of ninety bicycles. So the library accounted for two thirds of that combined total. Its share was also two thirds in the first survey, even though the total count was lower then.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Correct. State what the denominator is. You are comparing each building's count with the total for these two locations, not with every bicycle on campus. Also, don't call these figures occupancy rates. We did not measure the number of parking spaces available.

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: We counted at noon each day, so the times were consistent. At first I wanted to count whenever we had a free hour, but that might have introduced a time-of-day difference.

segments.speaker: Leila
segments.text: We used five-day averages because a single unusually busy day could distort the comparison. There was a sports tournament on the Friday of the second survey, for example. That day's sports centre count was above its usual level.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Explain that in your methods section. Now, you mention the cycle lane that opened between the surveys. Can you conclude that it caused the rise?

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: The timing fits, but we had no control site. Other things, such as weather or changes to car parking charges, might also have influenced the counts.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Exactly. Describe the association and acknowledge the limitation. Your evidence does not isolate the effect of the cycle lane. A future survey could include a comparable building that has no nearby new lane.

segments.speaker: Leila
segments.text: For the figure, we'll use grouped bars for the two years, with one group for each building. The vertical axis will start at zero, so the visual comparison isn't exaggerated.

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: I'll check the spreadsheet against our original count sheets. Leila will prepare the chart, and I'll write the methods and limitations.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Good. Submit the joint report by noon on Wednesday. Include clear units, identify both survey periods, and check that every comparison agrees with the figures.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 4: Total Consumption and Use per Plant

segments.speaker: Lecturer
segments.text: This lecture examines how the choice of measurement can change a report's conclusion. We will use a simulated teaching greenhouse to distinguish total consumption from consumption per plant. The question is simple: if the greenhouse uses more water, does that necessarily mean it has become less efficient? A total alone cannot answer that question.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: The gardeners recorded water in litres over two complete months, January and April. They used the same meter and checked its reading at the beginning and end of each month. In January, the greenhouse contained one hundred plants and used one thousand litres of water. The average was therefore ten litres per plant. That figure is an average across the whole collection, not a measurement of every individual plant.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: By April, the number of plants had risen to one hundred and fifty. Total water consumption was one thousand two hundred litres. Compared with January, the total had risen by two hundred litres, or twenty percent. A report that stopped there could leave readers with the impression that water use had simply become worse.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: However, dividing April's total by its one hundred and fifty plants gives eight litres per plant. The average had fallen from ten litres to eight, a reduction of twenty percent. Although total consumption rose, the amount per plant fell. These are compatible statements because they describe different indicators. One concerns the entire greenhouse; the other adjusts for the changing number of plants. Whenever you report a percentage, identify the denominator rather than assuming readers will infer it.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: There is another complication. In April, fifty of the one hundred and fifty plants were young, so young plants made up one third of the collection. In January, only twenty of the one hundred plants were young. The composition of the collection had therefore changed as well as its size. We do not have separate water measurements for the two age groups, so we cannot say how much of the change in the average was associated with that difference.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: A new hose was also installed between the two months. It would be premature to attribute the lower average entirely to the hose. There was no comparison with a control greenhouse, and the weather was warmer in April. The age composition and weather are possible confounding factors. These records describe changes, but they do not isolate the effect of one intervention.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: For next month's collection, I recommend recording water use separately for young and mature plants, while continuing to record the total. Keep notes about weather and equipment changes as well. The final report should present both total and per-plant figures, specify the periods and units, and distinguish an observed change from an explanation that still needs testing. Clear reporting can be more useful than a confident conclusion that the measurements do not support.
